set.post_content:
Not here to be liked is an art collective and design studio. We make work with and for the people and organisations that are changing the world.

What we do:

We make our own work. Installations and prints, shown at places like the Sainsbury Centre and the National Trust’s Dunham Massey. See our exhibitions.

We work with movements. Grassroots campaigns get identities, strategy, websites and training from us for little or nothing, because the groups who need good design most can least afford it.

We take commissions. Cultural institutions and NGOs hire us at our full rate, and that pays for the rest: every few days of paid work funds a day for a grassroots campaign. How that works.

Get in touch to start a project

Why we exist

We came out of the climate movement, where we worked as coordinators in Extinction Rebellion’s art, design and actions circles in its early years.

We started the studio in 2023 because of what we learned there. Good art and design help a movement get noticed and grow.

But their real power isn’t in changing people’s minds. It’s in giving people something to make and meaning to gather around, giving the press and the public something worth looking at, and leaving behind tools and skills the next group can use. The better it’s made, the more likely it is to be picked up.

The groups who need it most can least afford it.

How we work

We start most new collaborations – whether it’s with a civil resistance campaign or a cultural institution – with a point-of-view workshop. Before we design anything, we sit down with you to clarify what needs to be done, who you need to reach, and what would actually move them to act.

This all feeds into a research phase – looking at the people, places, contexts and history the work has to speak to – and only then do we move into making: concepts, drafts, feedback rounds, and finished work built on all these findings rather than our assumptions.

We occasionally do one-off projects with a quick turnaround and a clear brief, and offer ongoing support, strategic advice and workshops.

Who we are

Not here to be liked was founded in 2023 by Moa Pårup, Liam Geary Baulch and Erik Hartin.

LIAM GEARY BAULCH is an artist, activist, copywriter and campaign strategist who focuses on creating change through art and activism.

With over thirteen years of creative campaigning experience from healthcare and housing to combating the arms trade and the climate crisis, Liam has combined his activist and artistic praxis to achieve campaign wins like Save Lewisham Hospital and global attention-grabbing civil disobedience. As part of the team that launched Extinction Rebellion in 2018, Liam designed strategies for mass protest and impactful messaging from press stunts to social content.

MOA PÅRUP is an activist, designer and art director, working with direct action, print design and memes.

With many years of experience designing identities, books, magazines and exhibitions for clients within the cultural sector, Moa now designs campaigns and creates content for social movements. She co-coordinated the Extinction Rebellion UK Design Group between 2020 and 2023 and has a Master’s degree in Visual Communication from the Royal College of Art.

ERIK HARTIN is an activist-artist-researcher who specialises in visuals, tools and systems that help people act together.

With the artist collective Everyone Agrees he exhibited and published collectively written books. He has edited, designed and art-directed many books, magazines and websites since graduating from the Royal College of Art in 2011, and co-coordinated the Extinction Rebellion UK Design Group between 2020 and 2023.

Erik has been an Associate Lecturer at University of the Arts London since 2016 and is finishing a PhD on art and action in the Anthropocene at the University of East Anglia, where he is a Tyndall research fellow.

Collaborators

In 2025, CLIONA SHEPHARD worked with the studio on social media coordination and video editing. She still regularly contributes to our work.

We often work with Fletcher Horobin-Worley (Internal Garden) and Immo Klink. Other collaborators, past and present, include Hex Prints, The Edible Bus Stop and Absurd Intelligence.

We make visual identities, websites, posters and print, social media and installations for movements and cultural institutions. We also design actions, shape strategy, run workshops, give talks and show our own work in exhibitions.

Fund the work that can't pay for itself.

Protest that is well made gets seen, and gets pictured. But the groups who need that most are usually the ones who can least afford it. We exist to get it to them anyway – here's how you can help make that happen:

Fund us

Direct funding is the most powerful way to support this work. Grants let us decide where the need is greatest – taking on emerging grassroots groups, running workshops to help movements grow and sharpen strategies, and doing the often urgent and unfunded work that movements don’t have funds to pay for. In 2025 we received a grant to expand exactly this capacity and we're now looking to build on it with partners who fund movement infrastructure, cultural change or climate action.

Your support pays for:

  • Subsidised and pro-bono design, strategy and digital work for grassroots campaigns
  • Capacity to take on emerging groups who couldn't otherwise afford professional creative support
  • Workshops and trainings for groups and movements

If you fund this kind of work – directly, through a fiscal sponsor, or as a longer-term partner – we'd love to talk.

Get in touch about funding

Or hire us

Commissioning us is the other side of the same coin. When an organisation that can cover our full costs hires us, it directly funds the work we do for those who can't: every few days of paid work pays for a day given to a grassroots campaign. So a project with us isn't only a project: it's a website, an identity, a workshop or a campaign for you, and movement support you've made possible at the same time. We work with cultural institutions, NGOs and others who want their creative work to do double duty.

Get in touch to start a project
Explore our services

We've spent over a decade inside movements, not just designing for them: from coordinating Extinction Rebellion's design and social work, facilitating point-of-view workshops, teaching, to organising groups to make things together or run mass-trainings in action design for nonviolent protest groups. That experience is something we teach. We run sessions that help teams find their message, use design effectively, and work with everyone from grassroots campaigners to cultural institutions.

We build digital tools and strategies that do a job whether that is spreading a message, moving an audience, or quietly lowering its own carbon footprint while doing it. We've made full-stack websites and interactive artworks wired up to Raspberry Pis, run rapid-response social media experiments, and grown accounts from nothing to millions of views. We think strategically first and make the memes second (though we're very good at the memes). We develop and provide ongoing maintenance for full-stack web campaigns and sites, or deliver designs for implementation using online page builders. Ask nicely and we'll send the memes.

WHAT WE DO:

→Websites — design, build and hosting

→Carbon-light, accessible web (WCAG, A-rated)

→Social media strategy and content

→Rapid-response and reactive campaigns

→Copywriting and tone of voice

→Interactive and physical-digital installations

This website is run by Not here to be liked Ltd (company number 15356015). Our contact email if you need to ask us about this page or our data practices is welikeyou@nhtbl.studio.

What we collect

  • Newsletter. Your email address, and your name if share it. We store your contact details in Brevo, our mailing service, and use them only to send you the newsletter. Every email has an unsubscribe link.
  • Bot check. When you sign up, Cloudflare Turnstile checks that you are not a robot. It looks at technical details of your browser to do so.
  • Visitor numbers. We count visits with Plausible, which uses no cookies and does not identify you.
  • Emails you send us. We keep them for as long as we need to reply and work with you.

We do not use advertising or tracking cookies, and we would never under any circumstances sell or pass on your details.

Your rights

You can ask to see, correct or delete what we hold about you by emailing us. If you are unhappy with our answer, you can complain to the Information Commissioner’s Office at ico.org.uk.

Octopus Container (2025)
Not here to be liked

Steel shipping container, electronics, solar power system, 3D-printed replica of lost Lego octopus, fish tank, North Sea water, whale song, sea shanty, scientific facts, 3D-printed interpretation of Henry Moore's Mother and Child (1932), food colouring, water, water pumps, pipes, wood, paint, papier-mâché, printed materials

The installation uses a machine perception interface to configure itself in response to those who enter it. The container’s systems mimic octopus cognition – a distributed form of intelligence that reacts immediately to external environmental changes. One pathway into the space leads through grief towards the sound of the loneliest whale ‘singing’ to a plastic octopus, the sole survivor of the acid sea and the voice of Phoebe Plummer reading sections of the IPCC AR6. The other, in which a suspended sculpture of an octopus pours black liquid onto a 3D-printed interpretation of Henry Moore’s Mother and Child (1932), currently on view at the Sainsbury Centre. The installation draws from protest vocabulary and aesthetics to present a call for collective action in museums through resistance and song.
